chapter: Ch 5 — Acceptance of Deposits by Companies

questions.stem: Under section 2(31) of the Companies Act 2013, the expression “deposit”:

readLink.label: Read: What section 2(31) calls a deposit →

options.text: means only money received by a company from the public against a deposit receipt issued in the prescribed form
options.explanation: Far too narrow. The definition is inclusive and does not turn on who pays or on the issue of a receipt; a receipt in any form is caught.

options.text: means any money borrowed by a company, including a term loan taken from a banking company
options.explanation: Chapter V does not regulate borrowing generally. A loan or facility from a banking company is expressly taken out of the definition by rule 2(1)(c).

options.text: includes any receipt of money by way of deposit or loan or in any other form by a company, but does not include such categories of amount as may be prescribed in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India
options.explanation: Correct. Section 2(31) is inclusive at the front — “deposit or loan or in any other form” — and narrow at the back, the exclusions being prescribed by rule 2(1)(c) in consultation with the RBI.

options.text: means any amount received by a company which is repayable with interest
options.explanation: Interest is irrelevant to the definition. A non-interest-bearing receipt can be a deposit, and an interest-bearing one can be excluded.

questions.stem: Which of the following receipts is NOT excluded from the definition of deposit by rule 2(1)(c) of the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014?

readLink.label: Read: The exclusion list — rule 2(1)(c) →

options.text: ₹40 lakh received by a company as an interest-free loan from a partnership firm in which its managing director is a partner
options.explanation: Correct. A firm is not a company, so the inter-corporate limb does not apply; and the money comes from the firm, not from the director personally, so the director limb does not apply either. The receipt is a deposit.

options.text: ₹2 crore received from a State Government
options.explanation: Excluded absolutely — money from the Central or a State Government, money whose repayment they guarantee, and money from a local or statutory authority are all outside the definition.

options.text: A term loan received from a public financial institution notified by the Central Government
options.explanation: Excluded — loans or financial assistance from public financial institutions, regional financial institutions, insurance companies and scheduled banks are outside the definition.

options.text: A working-capital facility received from a co-operative bank
options.explanation: Excluded — the institutional-lender limb expressly covers banking companies and co-operative banks.

questions.stem: Sarvamangala Steels Limited receives ₹1.5 crore. In which of the following cases is the receipt excluded from the definition of deposit on the inter-corporate limb of rule 2(1)(c)?

readLink.label: Read: The exclusion list — rule 2(1)(c) →

options.text: The money is received from a limited liability partnership in which the company holds 60% of the capital
options.explanation: An LLP is a body corporate but it is not a company. The inter-corporate limb requires the payer to be a company; the degree of control is irrelevant.

options.text: The money is received from the sole proprietor of a firm that is the company’s largest supplier
options.explanation: An individual is not a company. Unless he happens to be a director (or, for a private company, a relative of a director) with the prescribed declaration, the receipt is a deposit.

options.text: The money is received from a private trust of which the company’s promoters are the beneficiaries
options.explanation: A trust is not a company. A separate exclusion covers non-interest-bearing money held IN trust by the company, which is a different situation altogether.

options.text: The money is received from another company, whether or not the two companies are related
options.explanation: Correct. The limb is stated at large — any amount received by a company from any other company — and no relationship, security or interest condition attaches to it.

questions.stem: Vaikhari Polymers Limited receives ₹80 lakh as share application money on 10 March 2026. No securities are allotted against it. To keep the amount outside the definition of deposit, the company must refund it on or before:
questions.sourceRef: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rule 2(1)(c) — 60 days to allot, 15 days to refund

readLink.label: Read: The exclusion list — rule 2(1)(c) →

options.explanation: That is the last day of the 60-day allotment window, not the refund date. Failure to allot by then does not by itself create a deposit — a further 15 days are allowed to refund.
Correct. 60 days from 10 March 2026 expire on 9 May 2026; the money must then be refunded within 15 days from that expiry, that is by 24 May 2026. Thereafter it is treated as a deposit.

options.text: 8 June 2026
options.explanation: That allows 30 days to refund after the 60 days. The rule allows 15 days, not 30.
That reads the 60 days as two calendar months from receipt. The rule counts 60 DAYS from the date of receipt of the money.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · Rule 2(1)(c) · Money from a director
questions.stem: Money received by a company from a person who was its director at the time of receipt is excluded from the definition of deposit only if:

readLink.label: Read: The exclusion list — rule 2(1)(c) →

options.text: the director furnishes to the company, at the time of giving the money, a written declaration that the amount is not being given out of funds acquired by him by borrowing or accepting loans or deposits from others, and the company discloses the details in the Board’s report
options.explanation: Correct. The three working conditions are: director at the time of receipt, an own-funds declaration in writing, and disclosure in the Board’s report.

options.text: the money is given free of interest and is repayable on demand
options.explanation: Neither condition appears in the rule. A director may lend at interest and the exclusion still holds; the terms of repayment are irrelevant to it.

options.text: the Board passes a resolution accepting the money and the amount does not exceed the director’s annual remuneration
options.explanation: The annual-salary ceiling belongs to the EMPLOYEE security-deposit exclusion, not to the director limb, and no Board resolution is prescribed as a condition of the exclusion.

options.text: the director holds at least 5% of the paid-up share capital of the company
options.explanation: No shareholding threshold exists. What matters is that he was a director when the money was received.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · Rule 2(1)(c) · Relative of a director
questions.stem: Rohini Agro Limited, a public company, and Rohini Foods Private Limited each receive ₹30 lakh from the brother of one of their directors, who furnishes the prescribed written declaration in each case. Which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: The exclusion list — rule 2(1)(c) →

options.text: The receipt is excluded for both companies, the prescribed declaration having been furnished
options.explanation: The declaration is necessary but not sufficient. The relative limb itself is not available to a public company, so no declaration can save the receipt for Rohini Agro Limited.

options.text: The receipt is a deposit for both companies, because the payer is not himself a director
options.explanation: That ignores the relative limb altogether, which is expressly available to a private company.

options.text: The receipt is excluded for Rohini Foods Private Limited but is a deposit for Rohini Agro Limited, because the relative-of-a-director limb is available to private companies only
options.explanation: Correct. The rule extends the exclusion to a relative of a director only in the case of a private company; a public company taking money from a director’s relative is taking a deposit.

options.text: The receipt is excluded for Rohini Agro Limited but not for Rohini Foods Private Limited, a private company being subject to stricter conditions
options.explanation: The position is exactly the reverse. The relaxation runs in favour of the private company.

questions.stem: Prathama Engineering Limited accepts an advance of ₹65 lakh on 5 May 2026 against the supply of goods. The last date by which the advance must be appropriated against supply if it is not to become a deposit is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rule 2(1)(c) — 365 days from acceptance

readLink.label: Read: The exclusion list — rule 2(1)(c) →

options.text: 5 November 2026
options.explanation: That is six months. The rule allows 365 days from the date of acceptance of the advance.
Correct. 365 days counted from 5 May 2026 land on 5 May 2027, the period spanning no 29 February.
An off-by-one count. The 365 days run from and exclude the date of acceptance, so day 365 is 5 May 2027.
That is two years. No two-year window exists for an advance against the supply of goods or services.

questions.stem: Which of the following advances falls OUTSIDE the business-advance exclusion in rule 2(1)(c)?

readLink.label: Read: The exclusion list — rule 2(1)(c) →

options.text: An advance received towards the consideration for an immovable property under an agreement, to be adjusted against the property in accordance with its terms
options.explanation: Expressly excluded. No 365-day clock applies to an immovable-property advance; the condition is adjustment against the property per the agreement.

options.text: A security deposit taken for the performance of a contract for the supply of goods
options.explanation: Expressly excluded as a performance security. Its duration is governed by the contract, not by the 365-day rule.

options.text: An advance received under a long-term project for the supply of capital goods
options.explanation: Expressly excluded, other than where the advance is one towards immovable property, which has its own entry.

options.text: An advance received from a customer towards a maintenance contract running for eight years, where common business practice in that trade is a three-year term
options.explanation: Correct. The warranty or maintenance limb is capped at the period prevalent in common business practice or five years, WHICHEVER IS LESS — here three years. An eight-year advance falls outside the exclusion.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · Rule 2(1)(c) proviso · Want of permission
questions.stem: An advance received against the supply of goods becomes refundable because the company does not hold the licence required to deal in those goods. The amount is treated as a deposit:
questions.sourceRef: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rule 2(1)(c) — proviso to the business-advance entries

readLink.label: Read: The exclusion list — rule 2(1)(c) →

options.text: immediately on receipt, the exclusion never having applied to it
options.explanation: The exclusion applies while the advance is a genuine trade advance. The proviso operates prospectively, once the money becomes refundable for want of the permission.

options.text: on the expiry of 365 days from the date of acceptance of the advance
options.explanation: The 365-day rule is the ordinary condition for an advance against goods or services. The proviso is a separate and earlier trigger, keyed to the refund becoming due.

options.text: after 15 days from the date on which it becomes due for refund
options.explanation: Correct. Where the amount becomes refundable because the company lacks a necessary permission or approval to deal in the goods, property or services, it is deemed a deposit 15 days after it falls due for refund.

options.text: only if the company fails to refund it within 30 days of a written demand by the payer
options.explanation: No 30-day period and no demand requirement appear in the proviso. The clock runs from the date the refund falls due.

questions.stem: Under a contract of employment, Sindhu Textiles Limited takes a non-interest-bearing security deposit from a supervisor whose annual salary is ₹7,20,000. The maximum amount the company may take from him without the receipt becoming a deposit is:

readLink.label: Read: The exclusion list — rule 2(1)(c) →

options.explanation: Correct. The exclusion covers a security deposit taken from an employee under his contract of employment not exceeding HIS ANNUAL SALARY, and it must be non-interest-bearing.
That is one month’s salary. The rule fixes the ceiling by reference to the annual salary, not a month’s pay.
That is half the annual salary. No such fraction appears in the rule.
That is twice the annual salary and exceeds the ceiling; the exclusion would be lost.

questions.stem: Which of the following issues of debt securities results in money that IS treated as a deposit?

readLink.label: Read: The exclusion list — rule 2(1)(c) →

options.text: Debentures secured by a first charge on the company’s land and buildings
options.explanation: Excluded — bonds or debentures secured by a first charge, or a charge ranking pari passu with the first charge, on the company’s tangible assets are outside the definition.

options.text: Unsecured, unlisted non-convertible debentures issued on a private placement basis
options.explanation: Correct. Unsecured NCDs escape the definition only if they are LISTED and issued in compliance with the applicable SEBI regulations. Unsecured and unlisted, the money is a deposit.

options.text: Bonds compulsorily convertible into shares of the company within ten years of issue
options.explanation: Excluded — compulsorily convertible instruments with a conversion window not exceeding ten years are outside the definition.

options.text: Listed non-convertible debentures issued in compliance with the applicable SEBI regulations
options.explanation: Excluded — this is precisely the listed-NCD limb, which does not require security.

questions.stem: An unsecured loan brought in by the promoters of Ashtavinayak Cements Limited in pursuance of a stipulation imposed by its lending bank stands excluded from the definition of deposit. That exclusion:

readLink.label: Read: The exclusion list — rule 2(1)(c) →

options.text: continues for the life of the company, the loan having been brought in at the bank’s instance
options.explanation: The exclusion is expressly time-limited. It does not survive the bank’s own loan.

options.text: continues so long as the promoters remain in control of the company
options.explanation: Control is irrelevant. The exclusion is tied to the subsistence of the lending institution’s loan, not to shareholding.

options.text: is available only if the loan is interest-free and is subordinated to the bank’s debt
options.explanation: Neither condition appears in the rule. The three real conditions concern the bank’s stipulation, the identity of the lender (promoters or their relatives) and the life of the bank loan.

options.text: is available only till the loans of the lending financial institution or bank are repaid, and not thereafter
options.explanation: Correct. The moment the bank’s loan is discharged, promoter money still outstanding with the company ceases to be excluded and becomes a deposit.

questions.stem: A convertible note issued by a start-up company is excluded from the definition of deposit where the amount received from a person in a single tranche is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rule 2(1)(c) — amendment-sensitive

readLink.label: Read: The exclusion list — rule 2(1)(c) →

options.text: any amount, provided the note converts into equity shares of the company
options.explanation: There is a monetary floor. A convertible note below it is not covered by this entry, however it converts.

options.text: ₹5 lakh or more, and repayable within five years of issue
options.explanation: Both figures are wrong on the position stated in these notes; the five-year window is the pre-amendment period.

options.text: ₹25 lakh or more, and convertible into equity shares or repayable within a period not exceeding ten years from the date of issue
options.explanation: Correct on the position stated in this chapter. Note the words “single tranche”: two smaller payments from the same investor are not aggregated to reach the floor.

options.text: ₹50 lakh or more, and convertible only on the next round of funding
options.explanation: No such threshold and no such trigger appear in the rule.

questions.stem: The prohibition in section 73(1) on inviting, accepting or renewing deposits from the public does not apply to:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 73(1) and its proviso

readLink.label: Read: Section 73 — the prohibition and deposits from members →

options.text: a banking company, a non-banking financial company registered with the Reserve Bank of India, and such other company as the Central Government may specify after consultation with the Reserve Bank
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso to s. 73(1) takes these companies outside the sub-section; they are regulated by the RBI instead.

options.text: any listed public company, whose disclosures are governed by the SEBI regulations
options.explanation: Listing confers no exemption. A listed company must still come through s. 73(2) or s. 76.

options.text: any private company, which is by definition prohibited from approaching the public
options.explanation: A private company is not exempt from Chapter V; it is simply outside s. 76, and its members’ deposits are governed by s. 73 read with the exemption notification.

options.text: any company whose deposits are fully secured by a charge on its assets
options.explanation: Security changes the character of the deposit, not the applicability of the section.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 73(2) · Conditions for members’ deposits
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a condition attached by section 73(2) to the acceptance of deposits from members?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 73(2) — clause (d) stands omitted

readLink.label: Read: Section 73 — the prohibition and deposits from members →

options.text: Issue of a circular to members showing the financial position of the company, the credit rating obtained, the total number of depositors and the amount due on earlier deposits
options.explanation: This is s. 73(2)(a), and it is a live condition.

options.text: Provision of deposit insurance in the prescribed manner in respect of every deposit accepted
options.explanation: Correct. Clause (d) of s. 73(2), which required deposit insurance, STANDS OMITTED; no insurance product was ever available and the compliance date was extended repeatedly before the clause was dropped. It is the standard distractor here.

options.text: Depositing, on or before 30 April each year, a sum not less than 20% of the deposits maturing during the following financial year in a deposit repayment reserve account with a scheduled bank
options.explanation: This is s. 73(2)(c), and it is a live condition.

options.text: Certifying that the company has not defaulted in the repayment of deposits or interest and, where a default did occur, that it was made good and five years have lapsed since
options.explanation: This is s. 73(2)(e), and it is a live condition.

questions.stem: A copy of the circular issued to members under section 73(2)(a), together with the statement it contains, must be filed with the Registrar:

readLink.label: Read: Section 73 — the prohibition and deposits from members →

options.text: within 30 days after the date of issue of the circular
options.explanation: The direction of the clock is reversed. The filing is a condition precedent to issue, not a return after it.

options.text: within 15 days after the first deposit is accepted
options.explanation: No such period exists. Fifteen days is the refund window in the share-application exclusion, not a filing period here.

options.text: along with the annual return of deposits in Form DPT-3
options.explanation: DPT-3 is an annual return filed by 30 June for the position as on 31 March. The circular has its own, earlier filing.

options.text: within 30 days before the date of issue of the circular
options.explanation: Correct. Section 73(2)(b) requires the circular and statement to be filed with the Registrar 30 days BEFORE the date of issue — a pre-filing.

questions.stem: Deposits of Vaidehi Papers Limited maturing during the following financial year amount to ₹6,25,00,000. The minimum sum the company must keep in its deposit repayment reserve account is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 73(2)(c) — 20% of deposits maturing in the following financial year

readLink.label: Read: Section 73 — the prohibition and deposits from members →

options.explanation: That is 25%. The statutory floor is 20%.
That is 15%, a figure that appears nowhere in the section.
Correct. 20% of ₹6,25,00,000, to be kept on or before 30 April in a separate account with a scheduled bank and used for nothing but the repayment of deposits.
That is 10%, which is the ceiling on short-term deposits under rule 3, not the reserve percentage.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · ss. 73(2)(c) and 73(5) · The reserve account
questions.stem: Which statement about the deposit repayment reserve account is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Section 73 — the prohibition and deposits from members →

options.text: The sum must be kept in a separate account with a scheduled bank and may not be used for any purpose other than the repayment of deposits
options.explanation: Correct. Section 73(2)(c) fixes the account and the bank; s. 73(5) forbids any other use, however pressing the company’s other obligations.

options.text: The sum may be applied to the company’s working capital so long as it is restored before the deposits mature
options.explanation: Section 73(5) admits no such temporary diversion. Any other use is a contravention.

options.text: The account may be maintained with any bank, and the balance may be used to pay any creditor of the company
options.explanation: Two errors: the bank must be a SCHEDULED bank, and the balance is reserved for depositors alone.

options.text: The account need be funded only in the financial year in which the deposits actually mature
options.explanation: The funding is made in advance — on or before 30 April, against deposits maturing in the following financial year.

questions.stem: Section 73(2)(e) requires the company to certify that it has not defaulted in the repayment of deposits or the interest on them. Where a default did occur, the company may accept deposits from its members only if:

readLink.label: Read: Section 73 — the prohibition and deposits from members →

options.text: the default has been made good and the depositor concerned has given his written consent
options.explanation: The consent of the affected depositor is not the test; the section fixes an objective waiting period.

options.text: the default has been made good and a period of five years has lapsed since the date of making good the default
options.explanation: Correct. Both limbs matter — the default must be cured, and five years must have run FROM the date of cure, not from the date of the default.

options.text: the default has been made good and a period of three years has lapsed since the date of the default
options.explanation: Both the period and its starting point are wrong: it is five years, running from the date the default was made good.

options.text: the Tribunal has, on an application by the company, condoned the default
options.explanation: No condonation route exists in s. 73(2)(e). The Tribunal’s roles under Chapter V are to hear a depositor under s. 73(4) and to extend time under s. 74(2).

questions.topic: Ch 5 · ss. 73(3) and 73(4) · The depositor’s remedy
questions.stem: Where a company fails to repay a deposit accepted under section 73(2), or the interest on it, the depositor’s remedy under section 73(4) is to apply to:

readLink.label: Read: Section 73 — the prohibition and deposits from members →

options.text: the Registrar of Companies, for a direction to the company to repay
options.explanation: The Registrar has no adjudicating power over a private claim of this kind.

options.text: the Regional Director, for compensation
options.explanation: The Regional Director exercises delegated Central Government powers elsewhere in the Act; he has no role under s. 73(4).

options.text: the Central Government, for an order winding up the company
options.explanation: Winding up is not the section’s remedy, and the Central Government is not its forum.

options.text: the Tribunal, for an order directing payment of the sum due or for any loss or damage incurred by reason of the non-payment, and for such other orders as the Tribunal deems fit
options.explanation: Correct. Section 73(4) gives the depositor a direct route to the NCLT, and the relief extends beyond the principal to loss or damage.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · Exemption notification · Private company ceiling
questions.stem: Shubhankar Foods Private Limited has paid-up share capital of ₹2,00,00,000, free reserves of ₹1,20,00,000 and a securities premium account of ₹80,00,000. Availing the exemption available to a private company of its class, the maximum amount of deposits it may accept from its members is:
questions.sourceRef: MCA exemption notification for private companies; Deposit Rules, rule 3(2) proviso

readLink.label: Read: Private companies — the relaxed route →

options.explanation: That is 35% of the base, which is the ceiling for a company accepting members’ deposits under s. 73(2) WITHOUT the private-company relaxation.
That takes the paid-up share capital alone. The base is capital PLUS free reserves PLUS the securities premium account.
Correct. Base = 2,00,00,000 + 1,20,00,000 + 80,00,000 = ₹4,00,00,000, and the exempt class permits members’ deposits up to 100% of that base.
That omits the securities premium account from the base. All three components count.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · Exemption notification · The exempt classes
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the classes of private company that the exemption notification relieves from clauses (a) to (e) of section 73(2)?
questions.sourceRef: MCA exemption notification dated 5 June 2015 as amended 13 June 2017 — amendment-sensitive

readLink.label: Read: Private companies — the relaxed route →

options.text: A private company all of whose members have given their written consent to the acceptance of the deposits
options.explanation: Correct. No such class exists. Unanimous member consent is not a route to the relaxation — the notification prescribes three specific classes and this is not one of them.

options.text: A private company which accepts from its members monies not exceeding 100% of the aggregate of its paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium account
options.explanation: This is the first class — the 100% company.

options.text: A private company which is a start-up, for ten years from the date of its incorporation
options.explanation: This is the second class, inserted by the 2017 amending notification and later extended from five years to ten.

options.text: A private company which is neither an associate nor a subsidiary of any other company, whose borrowings from banks, financial institutions or any body corporate are less than twice its paid-up share capital or ₹50 crore whichever is less, and which has not defaulted in repaying those borrowings
options.explanation: This is the third class, all three of whose conditions must be satisfied together.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · Exemption notification · What survives the relaxation
questions.stem: A private company that falls within an exempt class and accepts deposits from its members:
questions.sourceRef: MCA exemption notification, proviso; Deposit Rules, rule 16

readLink.label: Read: Private companies — the relaxed route →

options.text: is relieved of every filing under Chapter V, including the annual return of deposits
options.explanation: The relaxation is from the conditions in clauses (a) to (e) of s. 73(2), not from the return.

options.text: must nevertheless file the details of the monies so accepted with the Registrar, in the return of deposits in Form DPT-3
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso to the notification expressly preserves this filing, and rule 16 independently requires the annual DPT-3 return.

options.text: must still issue a circular in Form DPT-1 to its members and file it with the Registrar thirty days before issue
options.explanation: The circular requirement in clause (a) and its pre-filing in clause (b) are exactly what the relaxation removes.

options.text: may accept deposits from the public as well, provided it stays within the same ceiling
options.explanation: Never. Section 76 is open only to an eligible PUBLIC company; no private company may invite deposits from the public.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 76 · Who may approach the public
questions.stem: Which of the following companies may accept deposits from persons other than its members under section 76?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 76(1); Deposit Rules, rule 2(1)(e)

readLink.label: Read: Section 76 — eligible public companies →

options.text: A private company with a net worth of ₹260 crore, which passes a special resolution and files it with the Registrar before making the invitation
options.explanation: Size is irrelevant if the class is wrong. Section 76 speaks only of a PUBLIC company.

options.text: A public company with a net worth of ₹92 crore and a turnover of ₹410 crore, which passes a special resolution and files it with the Registrar before making the invitation
options.explanation: It fails BOTH financial limbs — net worth below ₹100 crore and turnover below ₹500 crore — so it is not an eligible company however impeccable its procedure.

options.text: A public company with a net worth of ₹140 crore, which passes the special resolution after the invitation is made and files it with the Registrar within thirty days
options.explanation: The financial limb is satisfied but the sequence is not: the resolution must be passed AND filed with the Registrar BEFORE any invitation to the public.

options.text: A public company with a net worth of ₹78 crore and a turnover of ₹540 crore, which passes a special resolution and files it with the Registrar before making the invitation
options.explanation: Correct. The two financial limbs are alternatives joined by OR, so the ₹540 crore turnover alone makes it eligible; and the resolution is passed and filed before the invitation.

questions.stem: Nirmalya Infrastructure Limited, an eligible company, has paid-up share capital of ₹60 crore, free reserves of ₹36 crore and a securities premium account of ₹24 crore. The maximum amount of deposits it may hold outstanding from persons other than its members is:

readLink.label: Read: Ceilings, tenure, interest and brokerage →

options.text: ₹30 crore
options.explanation: Correct. Base = 60 + 36 + 24 = ₹120 crore; deposits from the public are capped at 25% of that base.

options.text: ₹12 crore
options.explanation: That is 10% of the base, which is the ceiling on an eligible company’s deposits from its MEMBERS.

options.text: ₹42 crore
options.explanation: That is 35% — the members-plus-public aggregate an eligible company can reach, and separately the ceiling for a government eligible company. It is not the public-deposit limb by itself.

options.text: ₹24 crore
options.explanation: That is 25% of capital plus free reserves only. The securities premium account forms part of the base.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · Rule 3(3)(a) · Members’ ceiling for an eligible company
questions.stem: On the same figures (paid-up share capital ₹60 crore, free reserves ₹36 crore, securities premium ₹24 crore), Nirmalya Infrastructure Limited already has ₹6 crore of members’ deposits outstanding. The further amount it may accept from its members is:

readLink.label: Read: Ceilings, tenure, interest and brokerage →

options.text: ₹12 crore
options.explanation: That is the whole 10% ceiling. The test is applied to the proposed deposit TOGETHER WITH deposits already outstanding, so the ₹6 crore already taken must be deducted.

options.text: ₹6 crore
options.explanation: Correct. 10% of the ₹120 crore base is ₹12 crore; ₹6 crore is already outstanding, leaving headroom of ₹6 crore.

options.text: ₹36 crore
options.explanation: That applies the 35% figure. Thirty-five per cent is the members’ ceiling for a company that is NOT an eligible company, not for this one.

options.text: ₹24 crore
options.explanation: That applies the 25% public-deposit ceiling to money coming from members. The two limbs are separate.

questions.stem: The credit rating required of an eligible company accepting deposits from the public must be:

readLink.label: Read: Section 76 — eligible public companies →

options.text: obtained once, before the first invitation, and thereafter only if the terms of the deposits change
options.explanation: The proviso requires the rating to be refreshed every year during the tenure of the deposits, whether or not the terms change.

options.text: obtained from any two credit rating agencies and disclosed in the Board’s report
options.explanation: One recognised agency suffices, and the disclosure route is the circular and the return of deposits, not the Board’s report.

options.text: obtained from a recognised credit rating agency at the time of invitation and on every renewal, obtained every year during the tenure of the deposits, and a copy sent to the Registrar with the return of deposits
options.explanation: Correct. The rating covers the company’s net worth, liquidity and ability to pay its deposits on the due date, and it is an annual, continuing obligation.

options.text: obtained from the Reserve Bank of India before the circular is issued
options.explanation: The RBI does not rate companies. The rating comes from a recognised credit rating agency.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 76 proviso · Charge on secured deposits
questions.stem: A company accepting secured deposits from the public must create a charge on its assets in favour of the deposit holders:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 76(1), second proviso; Deposit Rules, rule 6

readLink.label: Read: Section 76 — eligible public companies →

options.text: within 7 days of the execution of the deposit trust deed
options.explanation: Seven days is the interval by which the deposit trust deed in Form DPT-2 must PRECEDE the circular, not a period for creating the charge.

options.text: within 60 days of the closure of the offer
options.explanation: No 60-day period applies. The clock runs from acceptance, not from closure.

options.text: within 30 days of the issue of the circular in the form of an advertisement
options.explanation: The right period, the wrong trigger. The 30 days run from the acceptance of the deposits.

options.text: within 30 days of the acceptance of the deposits, for an amount not less than the amount of deposits accepted
options.explanation: Correct. The charge must be created within 30 days of acceptance, on tangible assets, for an amount at least equal to the deposits accepted.

questions.stem: As to the tenure of deposits, the Deposit Rules provide that no company shall accept or renew any deposit:
questions.sourceRef: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rule 3(1) and 3(5)

readLink.label: Read: Ceilings, tenure, interest and brokerage →

options.text: repayable on demand, or repayable on notice within a period of less than six months or more than thirty-six months from the date of acceptance or renewal
options.explanation: Correct. The band is 6 to 36 months, and a deposit repayable on demand is forbidden outright.

options.text: for a period of less than twelve months or more than sixty months
options.explanation: Neither figure appears in the rule.

options.text: repayable on demand, unless the deposit is fully secured by a charge on the company’s assets
options.explanation: Security does not rescue an on-demand deposit; the prohibition applies to secured and unsecured deposits alike.

options.text: for a period exceeding twenty-four months, unless a credit rating is obtained
options.explanation: The outer limit is 36 months, and the credit rating relates to eligible companies accepting public deposits, not to tenure.

questions.stem: Ekanta Instruments Limited has paid-up share capital of ₹9 crore, free reserves of ₹4 crore and a securities premium account of ₹2 crore. To meet a short-term requirement of funds it wishes to accept deposits repayable earlier than six months. The maximum amount of such short-term deposits it may accept is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rule 3(1), proviso

readLink.label: Read: Ceilings, tenure, interest and brokerage →

options.text: ₹5.25 crore
options.explanation: That is 35% of the base — the members’ ceiling for a company under s. 73(2), not the short-term window.

options.text: ₹1.50 crore
options.explanation: Correct. Base = 9 + 4 + 2 = ₹15 crore, and short-term deposits repayable earlier than six months are capped at 10% of that base.

options.text: ₹3.75 crore
options.explanation: That is 25%, the public-deposit ceiling for an eligible company.

options.text: ₹90 lakh
options.explanation: That is 10% of the paid-up share capital alone. Free reserves and the securities premium account form part of the base.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · Rule 3(1) proviso · The three-month floor
questions.stem: Deposits accepted under the short-term exception to the six-month floor must, in addition to observing the ceiling on their amount:
questions.sourceRef: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rule 3(1), proviso

readLink.label: Read: Ceilings, tenure, interest and brokerage →

options.text: be repayable only after the company’s next annual general meeting
options.explanation: No such condition exists; the exception is keyed to time, not to a meeting.

options.text: carry no interest for the first three months
options.explanation: The exception does not touch interest. Interest remains capped by the RBI’s NBFC ceiling.

options.text: not be repayable earlier than three months from the date of the deposit or its renewal
options.explanation: Correct. The short-term window still has a floor: three months, not less.

options.text: be accepted only from members who have held their shares for at least three months
options.explanation: The exception says nothing about who may deposit or for how long he has been a member.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the terms on which deposits may be accepted is INCORRECT?

readLink.label: Read: Ceilings, tenure, interest and brokerage →

options.text: Deposits may be accepted in joint names not exceeding three
options.explanation: Correct as a statement of the rule — up to three names, with clauses such as “Jointly” or “Either or Survivor”.

options.text: The rate of interest may not exceed the maximum rate prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India for the acceptance of deposits by non-banking financial companies
options.explanation: Correct as a statement of the rule. The ceiling floats with the RBI rate; there is no fixed percentage in the Deposit Rules.

options.text: Brokerage paid to a person authorised to solicit deposits may not exceed the maximum brokerage so prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India, but legal, rating and advertisement expenses are not brokerage
options.explanation: Correct as a statement of the rule, including the exclusion of legal, rating and advertisement costs from “brokerage”.

options.text: A company may reserve to itself the right to alter the terms of a deposit after the circular has been issued, provided the depositor is given thirty days’ notice
options.explanation: Correct answer — this statement is FALSE. The rule forbids a company from reserving to itself, directly or indirectly, any right to alter the terms of the deposit, the trust deed or the insurance contract to the prejudice or disadvantage of the depositor. No notice period cures it.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · Rule 16 · The annual return DPT-3
questions.stem: The annual return of deposits of Haritha Agri Limited must furnish information as on 31 March 2027, duly audited by the company’s auditor. It must be filed with the Registrar on or before:

readLink.label: Read: Forms, filings and the register →

options.text: 30 June 2027
options.explanation: Correct. The return in Form DPT-3 is filed on or before 30 June of every year, carrying the position as on 31 March of that year, audited by the company’s auditor.

options.text: 30 April 2027
options.explanation: 30 April is the deadline for funding the deposit repayment reserve account under s. 73(2)(c), not for the return.

options.text: 30 September 2027
options.explanation: That is the outer date for holding an annual general meeting in an ordinary year; it has nothing to do with DPT-3.

options.text: 31 December 2027
options.explanation: No filing under the Deposit Rules falls due on this date.

questions.stem: The register of deposits required by the Deposit Rules must be:

readLink.label: Read: Forms, filings and the register →

options.text: kept at the corporate office and preserved for five years from the date of the last repayment
options.explanation: Both the place and the preservation period are wrong.

options.text: kept at the registered office, with entries made within seven days from the date of issue of the deposit receipt and authenticated by a director, the company secretary or an officer authorised by the Board, and preserved for not less than eight years from the financial year in which the latest entry is made
options.explanation: Correct on all three counts — place, the seven-day entry clock with authentication, and the eight-year preservation period.

options.text: kept at the registered office, with entries made within thirty days of acceptance and preserved for three years
options.explanation: The place is right; the seven-day entry clock and the eight-year preservation period are not.

options.text: kept by the deposit trustee and produced to the Registrar on demand
options.explanation: The deposit trustee holds the security for secured deposits; the register is the company’s own record, kept at its registered office.

questions.stem: A deposit of ₹15,00,000 accepted by Sharada Ceramics Limited matures and is claimed on 20 June 2026, but is repaid only on 1 September 2026. The penal interest payable for the overdue period is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rule 17 — 18% p.a. for the overdue period

readLink.label: Read: Repayment, premature repayment and penal interest →

options.explanation: That applies 12% to the 73-day overdue period. The prescribed penal rate is 18% per annum.
That applies 15%. The rule prescribes 18% per annum for the overdue period.
Correct. The overdue period is 73 days (10 days of June + 31 + 31 + 1). ₹15,00,000 × 18% × 73/365 = ₹54,000, payable over and above the principal and the contractual interest to maturity.
That charges 18% for a full year. Penal interest runs only for the overdue period.

questions.stem: A deposit of ₹5,00,000 was accepted for 36 months at 11% per annum. At the depositor’s request the company repays it after it has run 18 months. The company’s rate for a deposit accepted for 18 months is 9.5% per annum. The interest payable to the depositor is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rule 15 — rate for the period run, less 1%

readLink.label: Read: Repayment, premature repayment and penal interest →

options.explanation: That pays the contracted 11% for 18 months, ignoring the rule altogether.
That deducts 1% from the CONTRACTED rate (11% − 1% = 10%). The deduction is made from the rate for the period the deposit actually ran.
That uses 9.5% without the 1% reduction. The rule requires the rate for the period run to be reduced by one percentage point.
Correct. Rate for the period actually run = 9.5%, reduced by 1% → 8.5%. ₹5,00,000 × 8.5% × 18/12 = ₹63,750.

questions.stem: In respect of deposits accepted before the commencement of the Companies Act 2013 and remaining unpaid, section 74(1) requires the company to:

readLink.label: Read: Sections 74 and 75 — old deposits and damages for fraud →

options.text: file with the Registrar, within three months of the commencement or of the date on which the payments became due, a statement of all such deposits and the sums remaining unpaid with interest, together with the arrangements made for repayment, and to repay them within three years of the commencement or on or before the expiry of the period for which they were accepted, whichever is earlier
options.explanation: Correct. The statement is Form DPT-4, filed within three months; repayment follows the three-years-or-original-tenure-whichever-is-earlier rule.

options.text: repay them within one year of the commencement, no statement being required
options.explanation: The one-year period is the pre-amendment position and the statement requirement is not optional.

options.text: convert them into unsecured listed non-convertible debentures within six months
options.explanation: Section 74 provides no conversion route. A renewal must comply with Chapter V and the Rules.

options.text: obtain the approval of the Registrar for a repayment schedule, which may not exceed five years
options.explanation: Extension of time is granted by the TRIBUNAL under s. 74(2), not by the Registrar, and no five-year outer limit is prescribed.

questions.stem: Section 75 makes every officer of the company responsible for the acceptance of a deposit personally responsible, without any limitation of liability, for the losses or damages incurred by the depositors. That liability arises where:

readLink.label: Read: Sections 74 and 75 — old deposits and damages for fraud →

options.text: the company has failed to repay the deposit, whether or not any fraudulent purpose is shown
options.explanation: A mere failure to repay engages s. 73(4) and s. 76A. Section 75 needs more.

options.text: the company has failed to repay a deposit referred to in section 74 within the time allowed and it is proved that the deposits had been accepted with intent to defraud the depositors or for any fraudulent purpose
options.explanation: Correct. Both limbs are needed — failure within the time allowed AND proof of fraudulent intent — and the liability is without prejudice to s. 74(3) and to liability under s. 447.

options.text: the Tribunal has refused to grant the company further time to repay under section 74(2)
options.explanation: A refusal of further time is not the trigger; proof of fraudulent intent is.

options.text: the deposits were accepted without obtaining a credit rating
options.explanation: That is a contravention attracting s. 76A. It is not, without more, fraud under s. 75.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · Case: sorting the receipts of a private company
questions.case: Meghadoot Instruments Private Limited, incorporated in 2011, manufactures laboratory equipment. Its paid-up share capital is ₹1.50 crore, free reserves ₹90 lakh and securities premium ₹60 lakh. During the year ended 31 March 2028 it received: (i) ₹35 lakh from Mr Vasant, a director, who furnished a written declaration that the money was his own and not borrowed; (ii) ₹22 lakh from Mrs Vasant, his wife, who furnished the same declaration; (iii) ₹1.10 crore on 20 June 2027 from a hospital chain as an advance against calibration benches to be supplied later; (iv) ₹75 lakh from a developer as an advance towards the consideration for a plot the company has agreed to sell, to be adjusted against the property in accordance with the agreement; and (v) ₹40 lakh from Sahyadri Traders LLP, an affiliate of a supplier, as an interest-free loan.

readLink.label: Read: The exclusion list — rule 2(1)(c) →

questions.stem: Which of the five receipts is a deposit?

options.text: Receipt (i), because a loan from a director is a deposit unless the company is a public company
options.explanation: The director limb is available to every company, public or private, once the own-funds declaration is furnished. Receipt (i) is excluded.

options.text: Receipt (v), because a limited liability partnership is not a company and no other exclusion covers the receipt
options.explanation: Correct. The inter-corporate limb needs the payer to be a company; an LLP is a body corporate but not a company, and neither the director limb nor any business-advance limb applies to an interest-free loan from a supplier’s affiliate.

options.text: Receipt (ii), because the relative-of-a-director limb is not available to any company
options.explanation: It is available to a PRIVATE company, and Meghadoot Instruments is one. With the declaration furnished, receipt (ii) is excluded.

options.text: Receipt (iv), because every advance must be appropriated within 365 days
options.explanation: The 365-day rule applies to an advance against the supply of goods or services. An advance towards the consideration for immovable property has its own entry and its own condition.

questions.stem: The advance of ₹1.10 crore received on 20 June 2027 will escape being treated as a deposit only if it is appropriated against the supply of the calibration benches on or before:
questions.sourceRef: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rule 2(1)(c) — 365 days from acceptance

options.text: 20 June 2028
options.explanation: That reads the period as one calendar year. It is 365 DAYS, and the period from 20 June 2027 to 20 June 2028 spans 29 February 2028, so it runs to 366 days.

options.text: 20 December 2027
options.explanation: That is six months. The rule allows 365 days.

options.text: 19 June 2028
options.explanation: Correct. 365 days from 20 June 2027, the count including the leap day of 29 February 2028, end on 19 June 2028.

options.text: 31 March 2028
options.explanation: The financial-year end is irrelevant; the clock runs from the date the advance was accepted.

questions.stem: The advance of ₹75 lakh received against the plot the company has agreed to sell:

options.text: is excluded from the definition of deposit so long as it is adjusted against the immovable property in accordance with the terms of the agreement, no 365-day limit applying to it
options.explanation: Correct. The immovable-property entry is conditioned on adjustment against the property per the agreement, and carries no 365-day clock.

options.text: must also be adjusted within 365 days of receipt, failing which it becomes a deposit
options.explanation: The 365-day condition belongs to the advance-against-goods-or-services entry, not to this one.

options.text: is a deposit, because a company manufacturing laboratory equipment cannot deal in immovable property
options.explanation: The exclusion is not confined to companies in the real-estate business; it turns on the agreement and the adjustment.

options.text: is excluded only if the company creates a charge on the plot in favour of the payer within thirty days
options.explanation: The 30-day charge requirement relates to SECURED deposits accepted from the public under s. 76, not to a property advance.

questions.stem: Because it falls within an exempt class of private company, Meghadoot Instruments Private Limited:
questions.sourceRef: MCA exemption notification for private companies; Deposit Rules, rule 16

options.text: is relieved of every requirement of Chapter V, including the maintenance of a register of deposits
options.explanation: The relaxation touches only clauses (a) to (e) of s. 73(2). The register of deposits, the tenure band and the repayment obligations all continue to apply.

options.text: may, being exempt, invite deposits from the public as well as from its members
options.explanation: No private company may invite deposits from the public. Section 76 is confined to eligible PUBLIC companies.

options.text: must still issue a circular in Form DPT-1 to its members and file it with the Registrar thirty days before issue
options.explanation: The circular in clause (a) and its pre-filing in clause (b) are precisely what the exemption removes.

options.text: is relieved of clauses (a) to (e) of section 73(2), but must still file the details of the monies accepted with the Registrar in Form DPT-3
options.explanation: Correct. The relaxation is procedural and partial; the return of deposits survives it, as the proviso to the notification expressly states.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · Case: an eligible company that jumped the gun
questions.case: Girinagar Textiles Limited is a public company with paid-up share capital of ₹40 crore, free reserves of ₹24 crore and a securities premium account of ₹16 crore. Its audited accounts for the year ended 31 March 2027 show a net worth of ₹86 crore and a turnover of ₹560 crore. On 8 June 2027 the Board resolves to invite deposits from the public. Advertisements are issued and ₹35 lakh is collected from 180 members of the public between 12 June 2027 and 30 June 2027. The members pass a special resolution only on 22 June 2027, and the company files it with the Registrar on 5 July 2027. Two of the depositors are not repaid on the due date.

readLink.label: Read: Section 76 — eligible public companies →

questions.stem: Judged on its financial size alone, Girinagar Textiles Limited:

options.text: is not an eligible company, because its net worth is below ₹100 crore
options.explanation: The net-worth limb is not the only route. A turnover of ₹500 crore or more independently satisfies the test.

options.text: is not an eligible company, because both the net worth and the turnover tests must be satisfied
options.explanation: The two limbs are joined by OR, not AND. Either one suffices.

options.text: is an eligible company, because its paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium together exceed ₹50 crore
options.explanation: That aggregate is the BASE for the percentage ceilings. It is not the eligibility test.

options.text: is an eligible company, because the turnover of ₹560 crore satisfies the ₹500 crore limb, the two limbs being alternatives
options.explanation: Correct. Net worth ₹86 crore fails the ₹100 crore limb, but the turnover limb is independently satisfied, so the company is an eligible company.

questions.stem: The deposits collected between 12 June and 30 June 2027 were collected:
questions.sourceRef: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rule 2(1)(e); Companies Act 2013, s. 76(1)

options.text: in contravention of the requirements, because the prior consent of the members by special resolution must be obtained AND the resolution filed with the Registrar before any invitation to the public is made
options.explanation: Correct. Eligibility is not merely a financial test: the special resolution must be passed and filed with the Registrar before the invitation. Here the collection preceded both.

options.text: validly, because the special resolution was passed within the same financial year in which the deposits were collected
options.explanation: The rule fixes a sequence, not a financial year. Passing the resolution afterwards does not cure an invitation already made.

options.text: validly, because the Board resolution of 8 June 2027 authorised the invitation
options.explanation: A Board resolution cannot substitute for the members’ prior consent, nor for the filing with the Registrar.

options.text: in contravention of the requirements only if the deposits exceeded the limits specified in section 180(1)(c)
options.explanation: Staying inside the s. 180(1)(c) limits merely lets an ORDINARY resolution replace the special one. It does not dispense with the resolution or with filing it before the invitation.

questions.stem: In addition to obtaining and filing the members’ resolution before the invitation, the company must:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 76(1), provisos; Deposit Rules, rule 6

options.text: obtain a credit rating once before the first invitation, and create a charge on its assets within sixty days of accepting any secured deposits
options.explanation: The rating is an annual obligation, and the charge must be created within thirty days of acceptance, not sixty.

options.text: obtain a credit rating from the Reserve Bank of India annually and file it with the Registrar in Form DPT-1
options.explanation: Ratings come from a recognised credit rating agency, not the RBI, and the copy goes to the Registrar with the return of deposits, not with the circular.

options.text: obtain a rating from a recognised credit rating agency at the time of invitation, on every renewal and every year during the tenure of the deposits, send a copy to the Registrar with the return of deposits, and, for secured deposits, create a charge on its assets within thirty days of acceptance
options.explanation: Correct. These are the two continuing obligations the provisos to s. 76(1) add on top of every s. 73(2) condition.

options.text: obtain the prior approval of the Tribunal for the amount and tenure of the deposits
options.explanation: The Tribunal has no approving role. Its Chapter V functions are to hear a depositor under s. 73(4) and to extend time under s. 74(2).

questions.stem: For accepting the ₹35 lakh in contravention of the manner and conditions prescribed, the minimum penalty payable by the company under section 76A, over and above repaying the deposits with interest, is:

options.explanation: That treats ₹1 crore as a floor in every case. The section takes the LOWER of ₹1 crore and twice the deposits accepted.
Correct. Twice the deposits accepted = 2 × ₹35,00,000 = ₹70,00,000, which is lower than ₹1 crore, so ₹70,00,000 is the minimum; the outer limit of ₹10 crore does not bite.
That is the deposit itself, which the company must repay with interest anyway. The penalty is in ADDITION to repayment.
That is the statutory ceiling, not the minimum.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · Case: a non-eligible public company taking members’ deposits
questions.case: Vaidehi Papers Limited is a public company that is not an eligible company. Its paid-up share capital is ₹8 crore, its free reserves ₹3.50 crore and its securities premium account ₹2.50 crore. It already has ₹1.40 crore of members’ deposits outstanding and proposes to accept more from its members. Deposits amounting to ₹4.60 crore mature during the following financial year. The company had defaulted in paying interest on deposits in an earlier year and made that default good on 9 March 2023; there has been no default since.

readLink.label: Read: Section 73 — the prohibition and deposits from members →

questions.stem: The further amount Vaidehi Papers Limited may accept from its members without breaching the prescribed ceiling is:

options.explanation: That is the whole 35% ceiling. The ceiling is tested on the proposed deposit TOGETHER WITH deposits already outstanding, so the ₹1.40 crore already held must be deducted.
That applies the 100% ceiling, which is available only to a private company within an exempt class. Vaidehi Papers is a public company.
Correct. Base = 8.00 + 3.50 + 2.50 = ₹14 crore; 35% of that is ₹4.90 crore; less ₹1.40 crore already outstanding leaves ₹3.50 crore.
That applies the 10% ceiling, which governs an ELIGIBLE company’s deposits from its members. This company is not an eligible company.

questions.stem: Against the ₹4.60 crore of deposits maturing during the following financial year, the company must keep in its deposit repayment reserve account a sum of not less than:

options.explanation: That is 25%. The statutory floor is 20%.
Correct. 20% of ₹4,60,00,000, to be kept on or before 30 April in a separate account with a scheduled bank, and usable only for the repayment of deposits.
That is 10%, the short-term-deposit ceiling under rule 3, not the reserve percentage.
That is 35%, the members’ deposit ceiling, which has nothing to do with the reserve account.

questions.stem: As to the default in payment of deposit interest that the company made good on 9 March 2023, section 73(2)(e) requires that:

options.text: a period of five years must have lapsed from the date on which the default was made good before the company accepts deposits from its members
options.explanation: Correct. The certification under s. 73(2)(e) is available only where the default has been made good AND five years have lapsed from the date of making it good.

options.text: a period of three years must have lapsed from the date of the default
options.explanation: Both the length of the period and its starting point are wrong.

options.text: the company obtain the written consent of the depositor who suffered the default
options.explanation: The section prescribes an objective waiting period, not the consent of the affected depositor.

options.text: the company disclose the default in the circular issued to members, no waiting period being prescribed
options.explanation: Disclosure in the circular is a separate obligation under s. 73(2)(a). It does not displace the five-year wait.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 2(31) and rule 2(1)(c) · Meaning of deposit and the exclusions
questions.stem: Define “deposit” under the Companies Act 2013 and state, with the conditions attached to each, any five categories of amount received by a company that are not treated as deposits under the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 2(31): a deposit INCLUDES any receipt of money by way of deposit or loan or in any other form by a company, but does not include such categories of amount as may be prescribed in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India — an inclusive definition, so the label the parties use is irrelevant
The exclusions are prescribed by rule 2(1)(c) of the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, made in consultation with the RBI; they are rules-level and have been amended repeatedly

Any five, each with its condition, for example: money from the Central or a State Government or guaranteed by them, or from a local or statutory authority (absolute); a loan or facility from a banking company, co-operative bank, public financial institution, scheduled bank or insurance company; any amount received from any other company; share application money pending allotment, subject to allotment within 60 days and refund within 15 days thereafter; money from a director (and, for a private company, a relative of a director) with a written own-funds declaration and disclosure in the Board's report

Further examples available for credit: secured bonds or debentures, compulsorily convertible bonds with a conversion window not exceeding ten years, and listed non-convertible debentures; an employee security deposit not exceeding his annual salary and non-interest-bearing; a business advance against goods or services appropriated within 365 days; promoters' unsecured loans under a bank stipulation, only till the bank loan is repaid; a start-up convertible note of ₹25 lakh or more in a single tranche

questions.stem: Explain the conditions subject to which a company may accept deposits from its members under section 73 of the Companies Act 2013, and state the remedy available to a depositor who is not repaid. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 73(1): no company shall invite, accept or renew deposits from the public except as provided in Chapter V; the proviso excludes a banking company, an RBI-registered non-banking financial company and such other company as the Central Government may specify after consultation with the RBI
Section 73(2): deposits may be accepted from MEMBERS on terms agreed, including security if any, subject to a resolution passed in general meeting and to the prescribed rules

Condition (a): issue of a circular to members showing the financial position of the company, the credit rating obtained, the total number of depositors and the amount due on any previous deposits, in the prescribed form (Form DPT-1)
Condition (b): filing a copy of the circular with the statement with the Registrar within thirty days BEFORE the date of issue of the circular

Condition (c): depositing, on or before 30 April each year, a sum not less than 20% of the deposits maturing during the following financial year in a separate deposit repayment reserve account with a scheduled bank; and condition (e): certifying no default in repayment of deposits or interest, and where a default occurred, that it was made good and five years have lapsed since. Clause (d) on deposit insurance stands omitted

Condition (f): providing security, if any, including creation of a charge on the company's property; deposits not secured or only partly secured are 'unsecured deposits'. Section 73(3): repayment with interest per the agreement. Section 73(4): on failure, the DEPOSITOR may apply to the Tribunal for payment of the sum due, for loss or damage, and for such other orders as the Tribunal deems fit. Section 73(5): the reserve account may be used for no purpose other than repayment of deposits

questions.stem: Money received by a company from its directors, from its employees, from its promoters and as a trade advance is excluded from the definition of deposit only on conditions. State those conditions in each case. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Directors: the payer must have been a director AT THE TIME the money was received; he must furnish a written declaration that the amount is not being given out of funds acquired by him by borrowing or accepting loans or deposits from others; and the company must disclose the details in the Board's report. In the case of a PRIVATE company the limb extends to a relative of a director on the same conditions; it does not so extend for a public company
Employees: the amount must be a security deposit taken under a contract of employment, must not exceed the employee's ANNUAL SALARY, and must be NON-INTEREST-BEARING; both limits are cumulative

Promoters: the unsecured loan must be brought in pursuance of a stipulation imposed by a lending financial institution or bank on the promoters to contribute such finance; it must be provided by the promoters themselves or their relatives or both; and the exemption is available only TILL the loan of the financial institution or bank is repaid, and not thereafter

Trade advances: an advance for the supply of goods or provision of services must be appropriated against supply within 365 days of acceptance; other listed advances (immovable property, performance security, long-term capital-goods projects, warranty or maintenance for the lesser of common business practice and five years, sectoral-regulator advances, publication subscriptions) carry their own conditions; and any such amount becoming refundable because the company lacks a necessary permission or approval is deemed a deposit 15 days after it falls due for refund
skeleton.citation: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rule 2(1)(c) and its proviso

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 76 · Eligible companies and deposits from the public
questions.stem: State who may accept deposits from persons other than its members under section 76 of the Companies Act 2013, the additional requirements such a company must satisfy, and the limits on the amount of deposits it may hold. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 76(1): notwithstanding section 73, a PUBLIC company having the prescribed net worth or turnover may accept deposits from persons other than its members, subject to compliance with the requirements of section 73(2) and the prescribed rules; section 76(2) applies the rest of Chapter V mutatis mutandis

Prescribed thresholds: a public company with a net worth of not less than ₹100 crore OR a turnover of not less than ₹500 crore — the limbs being alternatives; a private company is excluded whatever its size

Members' consent: prior consent by SPECIAL resolution in general meeting, the resolution being filed with the Registrar BEFORE any invitation to the public; an ORDINARY resolution suffices where the deposits are within the limits specified in section 180(1)(c)
skeleton.citation: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rule 2(1)(e), proviso; Companies Act 2013, s. 180(1)(c)

skeleton.point: Credit rating: a rating covering net worth, liquidity and ability to pay deposits on the due date, obtained from a recognised credit rating agency at the time of invitation and on every renewal, obtained EVERY YEAR during the tenure of the deposits, with a copy sent to the Registrar along with the return of deposits

Secured deposits: a charge on the company's tangible assets, of an amount not less than the deposits accepted, created in favour of the deposit holders within THIRTY DAYS of acceptance, with a deposit trustee appointed and a deposit trust deed executed at least seven days before the circular or advertisement is issued
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 76(1), second proviso; Deposit Rules, rules 6 and 7

skeleton.point: Ceilings on the base of paid-up share capital plus free reserves plus securities premium account: deposits from members not exceeding 10%, and deposits from persons other than members not exceeding 25%; for a Government company eligible under section 76, 35% in the aggregate
skeleton.citation: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rules 3(3) and 3(4)

questions.topic: Ch 5 · ss. 74, 75 and 76A · Old deposits, fraud and penalty
questions.stem: Explain the obligations of a company under section 74 in respect of deposits accepted before the commencement of the Companies Act 2013, the personal liability created by section 75, and the penalty imposed on the company by section 76A. (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 74(1)(a): file with the Registrar, within three months of the commencement of the Act or of the date on which the payments became due, a statement of all deposits accepted and the sums remaining unpaid with the interest payable, together with the arrangements made for repayment — Form DPT-4

Section 74(1)(b): repay the deposits within three years of the commencement, or on or before the expiry of the period for which they were accepted, whichever is earlier; any renewal must comply with Chapter V and the Rules. Section 74(2): the Tribunal may, on the company's application and after considering its financial condition, the amount involved and the interest payable, allow such further time as it considers reasonable

Section 75: where the company fails to repay within the time allowed AND it is proved that the deposits were accepted with intent to defraud the depositors or for any fraudulent purpose, every officer responsible for the acceptance is personally responsible, WITHOUT ANY LIMITATION OF LIABILITY, for the losses or damages incurred by the depositors, without prejudice to section 74(3) and liability under section 447; the action may be brought by any person, group of persons or association of persons who suffered loss

Section 76A: on acceptance or invitation in contravention of the manner or conditions prescribed under section 73 or 76 or the rules, or failure to repay in time, the company is liable, in addition to repaying the deposit and interest due, to a penalty of ₹1 crore or twice the amount of deposits accepted, WHICHEVER IS LOWER, extending to ₹10 crore; every officer in default faces imprisonment up to seven years and fine, and an officer who acted knowingly or wilfully with intent to deceive is liable under section 447

questions.topic: Ch 5 · Rules 3, 15, 16 and 17 · Ceilings, tenure and repayment
questions.stem: Sandhya Alloys Limited, a public company that is not an eligible company, has paid-up share capital of ₹10 crore, free reserves of ₹6 crore and a securities premium account of ₹4 crore. It proposes to accept deposits from its members for a term of 30 months, and also to accept some deposits repayable in four months to meet a short-term need. Advise the company on the maximum amounts it may accept, the tenure restrictions, the annual return it must file, and the consequences of repaying a matured deposit late or repaying one before maturity at the depositor's request. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Base for every ceiling = paid-up share capital + free reserves + securities premium account = 10 + 6 + 4 = ₹20 crore

Members' deposits for a company accepting under section 73(2) may not exceed 35% of the base, that is ₹7 crore, counting the proposed deposit together with deposits already outstanding on the date of acceptance or renewal
Tenure: no deposit repayable on demand, and none repayable on notice in less than six months or more than thirty-six months; the proposed 30-month term is within the band
skeleton.citation: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rules 3(1) and 3(5)

skeleton.point: Short-term exception: deposits repayable earlier than six months may be accepted for short-term requirements of funds, but only up to 10% of the base, that is ₹2 crore, and they must not be repayable earlier than three months from the date of deposit or renewal — so a four-month term is permissible within that ₹2 crore window
skeleton.citation: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rule 3(1), proviso

skeleton.point: Annual return: Form DPT-3 filed with the Registrar on or before 30 June of every year, furnishing information as on 31 March of that year, duly audited by the company's auditor; the return covers both deposits and receipts of money or loans not treated as deposits
skeleton.citation: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rules 16 and 16A

skeleton.point: Late repayment: penal interest at 18% per annum for the overdue period on a matured and claimed deposit, secured or unsecured, in addition to the principal and contractual interest. Premature repayment: not before six months have run; and where made after six months but before maturity, interest is payable at the rate the company would have paid had the deposit been accepted for the period it actually ran, REDUCED BY ONE PER CENT — no reduction applying where the depositor is instead permitted to renew
skeleton.citation: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules 2014, rules 15 and 17
